title: Cohort Rebalancer: adaptive timeout and fairness lab notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures exploratory experiments for a lightweight cohort-based rebalancer that adjusts per-cohort flush timeouts and slot allocation to improve tail latency and fairness across priority classes while preserving throughput. Goal is pragmatic: reduce p99 under mixed loads with small impact to median latency and utilization.

Background and motivation:
- Continuous batching currently uses a global timeout and urgency-weighted admission. We see repeated tail spikes when a small number of long sequences or high-urgency bursts monopolize early slots in microbatches.
- Prior notes looked at adaptive windowing and urgency weighting; this branch focuses on grouping requests into cohorts (arrival pattern + predicted token length bucket + priority) and tuning per-cohort flush timeouts and soft slot caps.
- Hypothesis: per-cohort timeouts let latency-sensitive cohorts flush slightly earlier without globally shrinking batch formation windows, preserving throughput for bulk cohorts. Cohort caps avoid starvation.

Experiment design:
- Environment: staging cluster with 4x A100-sim VMs (production-like kernel/resnet-disabled), 8 workers per VM, running runtime v0.18-cohort-exp.
- Workloads: synthetic mixed traces combining:
  * 60% bulk (embedding-like) small replies: mean tokens=16, poisson arrivals at 350rps
  * 30% interactive short: mean tokens=64, bursty (exponential interarrival)
  * 10% long converssational: mean tokens=512, tail heavy (p95 >> p50)
- Priority labels: normal and high-urgency. High-urgency is ~15% of interactive short.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 server token latency, request end-to-end latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, batch-size distribution, cohort starvation ratio (fraction of flushes where cohort had >0 queued but below slot cap for >timeout window), KV cache hit ratio. Traces collected via tracer v0.9 with 1ms resolution.

Configurations tested:
1) baseline-global: current prod-like single global timeout = 8ms, no cohort caps.
2) cohort-static: cohorts defined by (size_bucket, priority), timeouts: small=6ms, medium=8ms, long=20ms; slot_caps: small=12, medium=8, long=4.
3) cohort-adaptive-1: same cohorts; timeouts computed by EWMA of arrival interarrival with floor/ceiling; slot_caps dynamic scaled by recent occupancy (target utilization 70%).
4) cohort-adaptive-2 (aggressive fairness): reduce long-cohort slot caps by 50% and add demotion where long-cohort requests that wait >100ms get moved to background queue with reclamation policy.

Key results (summary numbers across 30-minute runs):
- Baseline-global:
  * p50=12.3ms, p95=48.1ms, p99=185.4ms, throughput=1.02M tokens/s, GPU util=82%
- Cohort-static:
  * p50=12.7ms, p95=39.2ms, p99=120.7ms, throughput=0.99M tokens/s, GPU util=78%
- Cohort-adaptive-1:
  * p50=13.1ms, p95=36.6ms, p99=105.2ms, throughput=0.98M tokens/s, GPU util=76%
- Cohort-adaptive-2:
  * p50=14.0ms, p95=34.9ms, p99=98.8ms, throughput=0.95M tokens/s, GPU util=73%
Observations:
- Both cohort strategies cut p99 by ~35-47% relative to baseline with modest throughput loss (3-7%).
- p50 increases by ~1-2ms as smaller cohorts flush earlier and overall batch formation is slightly less efficient; median impact acceptable for latency-sensitive features.
- GPU utilization decreases under stronger fairness caps; we saw more small-batch kernel invocations but still within acceptable cost envelope for staged customers.
- Cohort-adaptive-1 balanced p95 vs throughput best. Adaptive sizing responded well to bursty interactive traffic by temporarily increasing small-cohort slots.
- Aggressive demotion (adaptive-2) produced the best tail but penalized long conversation throughput noticeably; discussion needed whether demotion acceptable for SLAed long-tail workloads.

Profiling and bottleneck analysis:
- Traces show two dominant contributors to residual tail:
  1) scheduling scan time: per-flush cohort scanning (to respect caps and rebalancing) added ~0.6-1.2ms overhead in worst-case flush paths. This shows up as elevated first-byte latency for small cohorts under high concurrency.
  2) kernel launch latency on small batches: higher fraction of <8-token batches increased kernel launch overhead (measured ~0.9ms extra per small-batch).
- KV cache misses correlate with long-cohort p99s; long sequences with cold KV state amplified decode time. Adaptive-1 did slightly better by giving long-cohort more continuous slots when occupancy was high, improving cache locality.
- CPU-side serialization (protobuf and request unpack) contributed ~0.4ms median but negligible tail.
- Memory pressure and GC were not significant in these runs (heap steady).

Microtrace sample (excerpt):
- Request ID: r-20241105-1042
  * arrival queued->cohort assign: 0.02ms
  * queue wait: 58.1ms (long-conv)
  * flush-decision: 0.9ms (scan across 6 cohorts)
  * batch enqueue/kernels: 1.5ms
  * decode token stream: 42.3ms
  * end-to-end: 103.1ms
- This illustrates leftover long-conv wait dominates; demotion reduced occurrences in adaptive-2.

Open hypotheses / follow-ups:
- Reduce scan overhead: implement incremental cohort counters (O(1) checks) and avoid full cohort iteration on every flush. Expected to shave ~0.5-0.8ms from small-cohort flush path.
- Kernel fusion for small batches: investigate micro-kernel path that reduces launch overhead for <8-token batches; measure impact on throughput and power.
- Smarter demotion: move to probabilistic demotion based on observed tail risk score instead of fixed time threshold; test whether we can keep long-conv throughput while bounding tail.
- KV prefetch hints: for long conversations, pre-warm KV cache when a long sequence continues across requests (trace parent id).
- Adaptive slot smoothing: add hysteresis so slot_caps grow/shrink less aggressively to avoid oscillation under bursty traffic.

Action items (owners):
- Arjun: prototype incremental cohort counters and post perf microbench (due 2024-11-18).
- Maya: bench small-batch kernel path and prepare patch for fused launch + bench notes (due 2024-11-20).
- Liam: implement probabilistic demotion toggle behind feature flag and run A/B on staging (due 2024-11-22).
- Sofia: coordinate end-to-end perf dashboard for these cohorts and add blurred cost estimate (tokens/unit) for each config (due 2024-11-19).

Risks and decision points:
- Fairness vs cost: strong caps reduce tail at the expense of raw GPU efficiency; need product guidance on acceptable cost delta for Hosted API SLAs.
- Behavioral complexity: adaptive mechanisms add knobs; prefer simple defaults with opt-in aggressive fairness for enterprise tenants.

Notes to self / rough scribbles:
- Try alternate cohort axis: predicted completion time (model-based) instead of coarse size buckets.
- Consider integrating with routing policy: route high-urgency to dedicated low-latency pool when available (falls outside pure scheduler scope).
- Keep telemetry keys stable: cohort_id, slot_cap, last_growth_ts, demotion_count, eviction_reasons.

Appendix: quick command snippets used for traces collection
- run load: ./tools/stress-runner --trace-template mixed-cohorts.json --duration 1800 --workers 32
- collect tracer: curl -s http://staging-tracer/export?span=cohort_flush > traces.jsonl
- gpu util snapshot: watch -n1 nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv

End of notes.
